statement: A square of side 10 cm has a square of side 6 cm cut out of one corner, with the smaller square's sides lying along the larger one's. What is the area of the shape that remains?

choices.misconception: I gave the area of the piece that was removed rather than the piece that is left.
I counted only the 10 by 4 strip of the L shape and forgot the 4 by 6 piece.
I subtracted the side lengths, 10 - 6 = 4, and squared that.
I gave the area of the original square and forgot that anything had been cut away.

hints: Find both areas first, then take one from the other.
Work out the area of the whole square and of the square removed, then subtract. Never subtract side lengths and square afterwards.
The large square is 10 x 10 = 100 and the cut-out is 6 x 6 = 36.

solutions.reliable: The large square has area 100 and the removed square has area 36, so 64 square centimetres remain. The transferable idea: areas subtract but side lengths do not, so convert every length into an area before any subtraction happens.
solutions.elegant: The remaining shape splits into a 10 by 4 strip and a 4 by 6 rectangle, which is 40 + 24.

whyOnTest: Subtracting lengths and then squaring is the standard trap in shaded-area questions, and one distractor is exactly that answer.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
